title: Could One Odd Recoil Be a Higgsino?
hook: LUX-ZEPLIN saw a single 248 keV nuclear recoil it couldn't explain away. Two theorists point out that a TeV-mass Higgsino would produce exactly that kind of event — with no free parameters to tune.
key_points: LZ reported a 248 keV nuclear-recoil event of interest with no identified background explanation.
The authors propose a nearly pure Higgsino of about 1 TeV as an interpretation.
A Higgsino naturally comes as two nearly degenerate neutral Majorana states split by a small mass gap.
Their off-diagonal Z coupling makes the scattering inelastic — the incoming particle converts to the heavier state.
The same electroweak interaction fixes the cross section, so it is predicted rather than fitted.
For a mass splitting of about 350 keV, the predicted rate approaches LZ's published 90% confidence interval.
content_html: Dark matter experiments spend most of their lives reporting nothing. So when LUX-ZEPLIN flagged a single 248 keV nuclear-recoil event of interest, and studied a list of rare backgrounds and detector effects without landing on a likely explanation, theorists took notice.
extra_html: Katherine Freese and Dionysios Theodosopoulos propose an interpretation: a nearly pure Higgsino with a mass around 1 TeV. The appeal is that the scenario is tightly constrained rather than flexible. A Higgsino naturally supplies two nearly degenerate neutral Majorana states separated by a small mass splitting, and their off-diagonal coupling to the Z boson makes the scattering inelastic — the dark matter particle converts to the heavier state as it hits a nucleus. Inelastic scattering costs energy, which naturally pushes recoils to higher energies, and the same electroweak interaction that produces it fixes the cross section instead of leaving it as a knob to turn. The authors show that for a mass splitting of roughly 350 keV, the predicted inelastic Higgsino-nucleon cross section approaches LZ's published two-sided 90% confidence interval. One event is one event — but a candidate explanation that predicts its own rate is worth testing with more exposure.

related.title: LZ's One Unexplained Recoil
related.hook: The world's most sensitive dark matter detector widened its search window and found exactly one hard nuclear recoil where almost no background should be. Not a discovery — but not nothing either.

related.title: The Sun Says No to the Higgsino Explanation
related.hook: If a Higgsino caused LZ's odd recoil, the Sun would have been quietly hoovering up dark matter for billions of years — and IceCube would see the neutrinos. It doesn't.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: A Dark Matter Detector That Asks Which Way the Hit Came From
related.hook: Neutrons and dark matter can leave identical-looking recoils. MIMAC's answer: reconstruct the direction of each recoil and check whether it points where dark matter should come from.

related.title: Has Dark Matter Run Out of Good Ideas?
related.hook: Two philosophers of physics dissect how dark matter candidates get proposed — and argue the guiding principles that generated WIMPs, axions and the rest may have exhausted their heuristic steam.

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

flashcards.prompt: What makes 'inelastic' dark matter scattering different from the usual kind?
flashcards.back_html: The incoming particle converts into a slightly heavier partner state instead of just bouncing. That costs energy, so only fast-enough particles scatter, and the recoils are pushed to higher energies.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors emphasise that the Higgsino cross section is not a free parameter?

choices.text: It is fixed by the known electroweak Z coupling, so the model predicts the rate rather than fitting it
Because dark matter cross sections are always the same
Because LZ measured the cross section directly

flashcards.explanation_html: In a nearly pure Higgsino the off-diagonal Z coupling between the two nearly degenerate neutral states sets the inelastic scattering rate — a prediction, not a tuned input.

flashcards.prompt: What mass splitting brings the prediction close to LZ's reported interval?
flashcards.back_html: Roughly 350 keV, for a Higgsino of about 1 TeV.
